item.research_question: How does the addition of Al affect the microstructures and mechanical properties of CoCrFeMnNiAlx high-entropy alloy films?
item.processing_route: RF magnetron co-sputtering of CoCrFeMnNi alloy and Al targets; fixed power 400 W on CoCrFeMnNi target, Al target power varied 0–80 W; base pressure < 2.8 × 10–4 Pa; working pressure 0.4 Pa; Ar flow 20 sccm; deposition time 1.5 h; substrate rotation 14 rpm
item.test_conditions: Nanoindentation with Berkovich indenter (tip radius 150 nm); in-situ SEM micropillar compression tests at room temperature with strain rate 10–3 s–1; pillar aspect ratios 2.6–3.2; taper angles 2°–5°
key_findings: Hardness increased from 5.71 GPa (x=0) to 8.74 GPa (x=1.3)
Compressive yield strength increased from 1.59 GPa (x=0) to 3.73 GPa (x=1.3)
Fracture strength reached a maximum of 5.83 GPa at x=1.3
Fracture strain decreased from 20.91% (no fracture) to 13.78% as Al content increased
Phase transformation occurred from single FCC (x=0, 0.07) to duplex FCC+BCC (x=0.3, 0.6) to single BCC (x=1.0, 1.3)
Atomic size difference (δ) increased from ~1.1% to 5.33% with Al addition
Nanotwins were observed in FCC phases (x=0, 0.07, 0.3) but absent in single BCC phases (x=1.0, 1.3)
Film hardness was significantly higher than bulk counterparts due to smaller grain size and nanotwins
item.mechanism: The phase transition from FCC to BCC and the presence of nanotwins contribute to strengthening; the larger atomic radius of Al increases lattice distortion (atomic size difference), stabilizing the BCC structure; the high hardness and strength in films are attributed to much smaller grain size and the presence of nanotwins compared to bulk alloys; load drops in stress-strain curves are attributed to the pinning effect of dislocations by solute atoms.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.
item.future_work: The text does not explicitly state future work.
quotes: The hardness increased from 5.71 GPa at x = 0 to 8.74 GPa at x = 1.3.
Both nanotwins and BCC phase contributed to the strengthening effects for CoCrFeMnNiAlx HEAFs.

The crystalline structure changed from the single face-centered cubic (FCC) phase for x = 0 and 0.07 to duplex FCC + body-centered cubic (BCC) phases for x = 0.3 and 0.6, and eventually, to a single BCC phase for x = 1.0 and 1.3

records.text: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Al affect the microstructures and mechanical properties of CoCrFeMnNiAlx high-entropy alloy films?. System: CoCrFeMnNiAlx (x = 0, 0.07, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.3) high-entropy alloy films. Processing: RF magnetron co-sputtering of CoCrFeMnNi alloy and Al targets; fixed power 400 W on CoCrFeMnNi target, Al target power varied 0–80 W; base pressure < 2.8 × 10–4 Pa; working pressure 0.4 Pa; Ar flow 20 sccm; deposition time 1.5 h; substrate rotation 14 rpm. Test conditions: Nanoindentation with Berkovich indenter (tip radius 150 nm); in-situ SEM micropillar compression tests at room temperature with strain rate 10–3 s–1; pillar aspect ratios 2.6–3.2; taper angles 2°–5°. Findings: Hardness increased from 5.71 GPa (x=0) to 8.74 GPa (x=1.3); Compressive yield strength increased from 1.59 GPa (x=0) to 3.73 GPa (x=1.3); Fracture strength reached a maximum of 5.83 GPa at x=1.3; Fracture strain decreased from 20.91% (no fracture) to 13.78% as Al content increased; Phase transformation occurred from single FCC (x=0, 0.07) to duplex FCC+BCC (x=0.3, 0.6) to single BCC (x=1.0, 1.3); Atomic size difference (δ) increased from ~1.1% to 5.33% with Al addition; Nanotwins were observed in FCC phases (x=0, 0.07, 0.3) but absent in single BCC phases (x=1.0, 1.3); Film hardness was significantly higher than bulk counterparts due to smaller grain size and nanotwins. Mechanism: The phase transition from FCC to BCC and the presence of nanotwins contribute to strengthening; the larger atomic radius of Al increases lattice distortion (atomic size difference), stabilizing the BCC structure; the high hardness and strength in films are attributed to much smaller grain size and the presence of nanotwins compared to bulk alloys; load drops in stress-strain curves are attributed to the pinning effect of dislocations by solute atoms..
